name: FGL

lead: FGL is a 15-amino-acid peptide taken from NCAM, a protein involved in nerve-cell adhesion and plasticity. It was reported to activate the FGF receptor.
Studies are in cultured neurons and rodents, covering memory, ageing and Alzheimer's-type models. No human trials or appearance data were found.

paras: Reported to act as an FGFR1 agonist, promoting neurite outgrowth and neuronal survival in cultured rat neurons and changing synaptic structure in aged rats.
Human safety has not been established in published trials. It is not an approved drug, and animal findings do not establish human effects.

lead: FGL (the FG loop peptide) is a 15-amino-acid synthetic peptide derived from the second fibronectin type III module of the neural cell adhesion molecule (NCAM). It was reported to activate fibroblast growth factor receptor 1 (FGFR1), mimicking part of the signalling that NCAM performs during cell adhesion [1].

Published research is preclinical: primary rat neuron cultures, and rodent studies of memory, social recognition, ageing and Alzheimer's-type pathology [2][3][1][4][5][6][7]. No human clinical trial appears in the sources reviewed, and no data on appearance outcomes were found.
FGL is relevant to the wiki as a neuroactive peptide appearing in longevity and nootropic peptide catalogues; the sources reviewed contain no looksmaxxing community discussion of it.

paras: NCAM is involved in neural development, cell migration, synaptogenesis and synaptic plasticity, and signals through FGFR [3][8]. NCAM1 is a glycoprotein found on neurons, glia and skeletal muscle and is also known as CD56 [9]. FGL was reported to induce neurite outgrowth and neuronal survival in primary rat neurons [3], and in mice lacking NCAM it restored disrupted FGFR phosphorylation and signalling [10].

In rats given a beta-amyloid fragment to model early Alzheimer's-type changes, FGL reduced neuropathological signs and cognitive impairment [2]. Studies in rodents reported that FGL promoted early postnatal sensorimotor development and enhanced social memory retention [1], facilitated long-term plasticity in the dentate gyrus [7], altered synapse and dendritic spine structure in aged rats [5], modified age-related hippocampal changes [4], and affected spatial learning impairment after neonatal phencyclidine treatment [6]. A 2016 review discussed NCAM as a target for dysfunctional brain plasticity [8].
No studies found in humans. The research described above is in cells and animals and does not establish effects in people.
FGL is not an approved medicine in the sources reviewed. No community use or appearance claims were documented in them.
